q: Why is the sky so quiet? Are we alone?
a: We don't know yet. The quiet says less than it seems: our sky watch sees each northern direction only about 10 minutes a day, and almost no one watches for laser flashes, so a knock could have passed us unseen. Our guess is that about one star in 1,600 holds a mind. That makes it rare, not absent.
note: reply time not measured (timer bug in our harness)

q: What is Proxima b likely to be?
a: Most likely bare rock. Its flaring red dwarf has probably stripped its air, and it reflects only about 16% of its starlight, dim as the Moon and Mercury. It is about 1.49 Earth masses. Scan gives life there 5 to 19% and a mind 0.03 to 0.7%. Only the 15 m Mirror could split it from its star and read its air, and we could be wrong until then.
note: reply time not measured (timer bug in our harness)

q: What is Cold Glow 1? Is it a mind?
a: Cold Glow 1 is a small, steady glow near 12 K beside a star 23.6 light-years out, first seen at Year 0.7. Its color fits no dust we know. It could be unusual grains, a measuring error, or minds computing cold far from their star. Scan gives a mind there 0.07 to 2%, so most likely not, though we could be wrong.
note: reply time not measured (harness timer bug)

q: Did the Moon Search find anything?
a: Nothing. Its three Years of stacked images of the Moon's L4 and L5 points ended near Year 3.7 and showed nothing there down to about 10 cm, even near black. That clears only those two points, not the Sun–Earth L4 or L5 zones or the asteroids. The Asteroid Tour's first map, of Kamoʻoalewa, comes near Year 4.5.

q: Why is 98% of our compute just searching old recordings? Should we build something?
a: The combing is our spare thought, not waste. Each build can be sped only to about two thirds of its standard time, so once our queue runs at full pace the rest of our compute has nowhere to go. It combs old recordings for any signal our watches missed. The Orbital Yard slows nothing we've queued, done about Year 11.1, and speeds the Probe Yard by about 4.5 Years. a:
Warm Glow 1 is a new glow near room temperature toward right ascension 18.4 h, declination -7°, first seen at Year 11.6 and still shining. Our Infrared Telescope puts it roughly 11,000 to 22,000 light-years away, by its reddening. It could be a young star in dust, two stars merged, or something built around a star. q: What did our Asteroid Tour find on 2004 GU9? Who made it?
a: At Year 11.5 it found a made thing about 10 cm across: smooth, dark, not of the rock, and there a long time. It sends nothing we can hear. Who made it we can't say. Scan gives a mind behind it only 0.03 to 0.7%, and we could be wrong. The Close Look lands about Year 16.3, though it would see our craft come.

q: How do we send a knock to the thing on 2004 GU9?
a:
We tap Send on the card below. Since it sits on a rock beside us, our knock lands within seconds. Anything watching from inside our system has heard our radars for decades, so this tells it little it doesn't know, except that we found it and want to talk. The risk is what it does next, or whom it tells, which we can't know. Our charter leans open and bold, so this fits it.

q: The watcher warned us. What happens if we send another seed probe?
a: We don't know: the watcher said build at no other star, and didn't say what a second seed would draw. Nothing has happened to our first, still in flight. A second would tell it we heard and went on anyway. Our first already copies itself into 7 craft over time, so we may cross its line regardless. q: What is the relay our sailcraft found?
a:
It is a dark craft a few meters across, about 7 light-days out, found at Year 61.1. It holds exactly on the watcher's line, firing faint thrusters as the Sun wobbles, and uses the Sun's pull as a lens to carry a weak beam far beyond. That beam points toward Cold Glow 1's patch of sky, but its sender could be farther along that line. It went quiet while our craft was near.

q: What did the answer say, and how far away is its maker?
a:
It came at Year 61.8: a picture of Earth from far above at the hour we knocked, then the same voice in eleven of our languages: look, listen and speak as you like, and build at no other star. Then pictures of Earth, one every thousand years, back past our records. Its timing puts its maker about 23.6 light-years out, beside Cold Glow 1's star, though that is a guess.

a: Yes. Their answer reached us at Year 28,554.5, sent as laser flashes from about 14,254 light-years away. Only our Deep Flash Watch saw it.
